title: One-Line Rock Paper Scissors
tagline: A tiny Python game squeezed into two deliberately ridiculous lines
summary: A small code golf experiment to see how much game logic I could squeeze into as little code as possible without breaking it. The win, lose or tie logic fits on one line and the whole game loop on another. It's not a clean way to write a game, but finding the little Python tricks that made it fit was the whole point.

overview.what: A rock paper scissors game in Python where the whole thing fits on two lines: one for the win, lose or tie logic and one for the game loop.
overview.why: I wanted to see how much game logic I could squeeze into as little code as possible without breaking it.
overview.did: I turned the rock, paper, scissors triangle into list positions so a little math decides who wins, then used chained conditional expressions and semicolons to cram it all in.
overview.result: It works, and it's a terrible way to write a game, but finding the Python tricks that made it fit was the whole point. You can play it right on this page.

hero.caption: The triangle behind the one-line win test: rock beats scissors, scissors beats paper, and paper beats rock.

sections.heading: The two lines
body: Rock paper scissors is a triangle, not a ranking: rock beats scissors, scissors beats paper, and paper beats rock. My code puts the choices in the list [paper, rock, scissors], so they're 0, 1 and 2, and each one beats the item one step ahead of it.

For paper and rock, adding one gives the choice they beat: 0 + 1 is rock, and 1 + 1 is scissors. Scissors wraps around, so subtracting two turns its 2 into paper's 0. If neither test matches, the same number means a tie, and anything else is a loss.
Chained conditional expressions pick the result text, and semicolons keep the whole input loop on one line. It's squished on purpose, but the triangle is the simple idea underneath it.
